idiom_name: tagged command struct + opcode dispatch table (hand-written or protobuf-c codec)
implementation_notes: C has neither polymorphism nor reflection, so the command base degrades to a struct whose first member is a stable opcode plus a bounded payload, and the invoker becomes a static table of function pointers indexed by that opcode (or a switch over it). Serialisation is hand-written or generated - a protobuf-c descriptor-based codec is the closest thing to a library - and the same generated code must be linked into both sides. The shared `int (*execute)(const struct cmd *)` signature replaces the virtual Execute, and the command stays a value that is copied, not an object graph. Embedding the base struct as the first member of each concrete command (and casting back in the table entry) is the C analogue of inheritance, and it is worth it only when the payload layouts differ enough that one common struct would be unreadable.
pitfalls: No runtime type information: opcodes are a manual, global contract - never renumber or reuse one, and validate the tag against the table and the payload length before casting, or a crafted message becomes an out-of-bounds read.
Embedding the base as first member only works while alignment and initial layout agree; use a fixed-width tag field and keep packing-dependent structs out of the wire format.
A hand-written decoder must own its allocation policy: decode into a size-bounded buffer or a caller-provided arena, never into stack space sized by a length field from the message.
